correctness.rationale: Counting paths by their last pre-switch event gives the two sums in (1): a last basal birth leaves j<N clock events before it, whereas a last clock step leaves m<ell births and an Erlang(ell−m,q) residual time. Only the basal path with no clock events contributes at order s^(−ell), recovering ell and k. For r≠q, the order-ell pole at −q has a nonzero m=0 contribution, and at −r the two potentially cancelling highest-order terms have residual factor 1+Λα/(q−r)=(Λ−1)r/(q−r), nonzero. At r=q the second sum has positive leading coefficient at order ell+N. These counts separate distinct and coincident poles, recover N, and label the rates except in the distinct-rate one-stage case. There the next coefficient difference factors by (x−1)(y−1) by subtracting the two sums of geometric polynomials; the remaining sum is strictly signed for ell≥2 and x≠y. At ell=1 the entire transform is symmetric; both labels are admissible since r,q>k, with exactly two assignments. This also proves the threshold-two remedy. The unamplified Erlang law has a single order-ell pole and no clock dependence, hence cannot be confused with any amplified law.
residual_risks: Exact-law structural result only, with an independent Erlang clock, zero initial count and no degradation; neither noisy-data identifiability nor stable pole extraction is established.

value.rationale: The result tells an investigator what an exact marginal timing law does and does not determine in a hidden-clock model. In particular it gives a concrete observation-design distinction: one threshold may confound two admissible rates, while the next threshold breaks precisely that confounding, without observing the clock. It also recovers hidden stage count away from the no-amplification boundary, which is stronger than reporting abstract phase-type nonuniqueness.
residual_risks: No practical inference precision follows; near-coincident poles or restricted physical dosage ranges can change practical recovery or admissible ambiguity.
